events.title: Bunny Flags is part of Steam Next Fest!
events.summary: We're so happy to share that Bunny Flags, our capture-the-flag roguelite, is part of Steam Next Fest from October 19 to 26.The free single-player demo (version 0.3.2) is live on Steam right now. Jump in and let us know what you think!And if you'd like to try the co-op version of the demo, coming very soon to Steam, message us! events.title: V0.3.2 of Bunny Flags is up on steam.
events.summary: Hey everyone! There is a new version 0.3.2 of Bunny Flags is up on steam! small udate but with one BIG CHANGE!! Here it goes!!: 1. Video settings: modify screen resolution and windows mode. 2. Fixed minor bugs. 3. MAYOR UPDATE: New start level rules: you no longer start with a flag and the game will wait for your input before you start. Please, play it and let us know what you think and we really hope you enjoy it!! :D

The most important change is that you can now open Settings directly from the pause menu. events.title: It's Time for a New Roguelite Fight!
events.summary: The community asked for runs with more identity, a different pace, and higher replayability, but what you also wanted was for us to bring back the enemies that made our beloved trilogy iconic. events.title: Demo Update v0.1.6: Bunny Flags Now in 5 New Languages!
events.summary: Hey soldiers!We just released version 0.1.6 with brand new localizations! Our goal is for everyone to enjoy the demo, so now you can play Bunny Flags in Spanish, Simplified Chinese, Japanese, Russian, and German!Need to switch languages? Right-click Bunny Flags Demo in your Steam Library → Properties → General → Language, and pick the one you want. events.title: Ronny Antares Is Back with the Score of Bunny Flags!!
events.summary: Did you know that the first Bunny Charms game had no music, just gunfire and a handful of sound effects, which was pretty normal for web games back in 2009? That changed in early 2011, when Bunny Charms made its return as Bunny Flags and shifted from a shooter to a tower defense game. Chilean composer Ronny Antares came on board and gave it its first real score, one that's still doing its job today: building tension right before every battle.
